prize_parts.citation: For showing how collateral constraints and asset prices amplify and propagate shocks, and thereby generate credit cycles.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1: B011 with Kiyotaki and Moore only. Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) show that credit limits tied to collateral values, together with collateral values that depend on credit, turn small temporary shocks into large and persistent fluctuations. The mechanism is general and tractable, and it has been extended and used as a building block for close to three decades. The originating paper has two authors, so the credit line is as clean as any on the shortlist. As an economic historian I also note that the mechanism describes a recurring pattern in credit booms and busts across periods, which suggests it captures something structural and not episode-specific. I do not count the six round-1 preferences for B011 as evidence of merit. The chair's observation that the lead equals the six-vote requirement, includes the chair and a frequent co-author, and is narrow seems right to me. My reasons are substantive: depth of the idea, durability, and a credit line that needs no arbitrary boundary drawing among many contributors. For the wording, I suggest keeping the citation on the collateral-price feedback mechanism and explicitly not claiming the bank-focused work recognised in 2022 or the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist accelerator. That answers the chair's request to say what is not being honoured.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged. The 2022 prize to Bernanke, Diamond and Dybvig covered banks and financial crises, and a committee could read credit-cycle amplification as adjacent ground that is already honoured. I think the collateral-feedback mechanism is distinct, but I cannot show that the committee will agree. The second reservation is identification. The collateral channel is established more as a modelling building block and as a pattern in crisis episodes than as a measured magnitude, and B005 has a more direct record of testing on firm-level data. Excluding Gertler and Gilchrist leaves the quantitative strand that carried the idea into policy models unrecognised. That is a real cost and I do not hide it. B005 is a close competitor, and the dispute between B011 and B005 is about attribution and overlap, not about whether either is serious science. My assessments rely on general knowledge, and I have not independently verified any source.

responses.point: Fredriksson prefers B005 and holds that the collateral channel is hard to identify directly, so a conceptually foundational but weakly identified model is a different kind of achievement from one with a long record of firm-level testing. The 2022 overlap also weighs more heavily with Fredriksson than the opening discussion allowed.
responses.response: The identification point is the most serious scientific objection to B011, and I list it as an uncertainty. I weigh it differently. The Nobel tradition has recognised mechanisms whose importance shows in how widely they were used and built upon, as well as in direct estimates of magnitudes. From my own field, I would add that long-run credit histories show the same amplification pattern across different institutional settings, which is indirect but independent support. I agree that B005 has the more direct micro-data confirmation. I treat that as a real advantage of B005 and not as a decisive one. If the committee judges that a prize should rest on directly measured effects, B005 is where I would go, and I would support it in a single-part prize.

responses.point: Friberg prefers B005 and distinguishes Helpman's credit for the heterogeneous-firm extensions from the monopolistic-competition base covered by Krugman's 2008 prize. He would anchor the citation on selection and reallocation across firms and suggests the pair is defensible even though Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum are not credited.
responses.response: This is the best version of the B005 case, and the wording discipline is right: a citation for the integration of firm heterogeneity into trade theory does not claim the empirical discovery of exporter premia. My remaining difficulty is that the Helpman-Melitz boundary depends on how one separates Helpman's marginal credit from 2008 and from his separate B020 entry. Melitz's credit is clear. Helpman's rests on the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple strand, which is real but narrower than his overall programme. Under B011 no comparable boundary has to be drawn between two named laureates. I read the two as close, and I rank B005 first among alternatives. I would not call the attribution issue decisive against it if the wording is as narrow as you propose.

responses.point: Hassler, as chair, prefers B011 for Kiyotaki and Moore alone, treats the Gertler-Gilchrist accelerator as a distinct line that the 2022 recognition partly covered, and acknowledges the boundary as a judgement. He accepts B005 as the alternative while asking for explicit discussion of the Helpman-Melitz boundary.
responses.response: I agree with the two-name scope, and in round 1 I moved to it because of your argument. I would add a caution about how the committee uses the point that the 2022 overlap concerns the accelerator lineage. That reading helps B011 only if the citation wording actually keeps to collateral-price feedback. I would therefore avoid the phrase 'financial frictions' in general and name the mechanism. I also note that you and I both list the Gertler boundary as open, so the committee should not treat it as settled. On B005, I agree that it needs the explicit Helpman-Melitz discussion you request. Because the six-vote threshold equals the current count, with the chair and a frequent co-author included, I do not read the count as showing that the discussion is finished.

responses.point: Teorell prefers B012, has said that Hassler's account moved him toward treating B011 as a serious alternative, and concedes that B005 and B011 have cleaner attribution than B012. He rests the B012 case on the theory and on later state-capacity work, not on the early cross-country regressions.
responses.response: I take that framing seriously, since B012 is my third-ranked and listed alternative. The state-capacity strand ties into the long-run development and historical evidence I know best, and a citation built on it would be stronger than one built on early cross-sectional regressions. Your own concessions are what keep me from moving it up. Identification and the dispersion of the field are weaker than for B011, and after 2024 the committee would have to argue explicitly what is new. If the six-vote requirement is not met by B011 and B005, I could support B012 in a single-part prize, but only with the narrow wording you describe and with the three names kept as they are.

responses.point: Boppart moved from B001 to B005 and states that the choice between B005 and B011 is closer than his opening ranks suggested. He would not add a third name to B011 and would not oppose a B011 configuration with the same level of attribution care.
responses.response: I agree that the choice is close, and your point about narrow wording for B005 is one I accept. Your move away from B001 matches my view that the Mian-Sufi evidence is credible but younger, with the weight of credit supply still debated. I disagree only on ordering. For me the clean two-author origin of B011 outweighs the more direct firm-level testing of B005, but I regard that as a judgement and not a scientific finding. Your remark that you would accept B011 with careful attribution matters to me, because it suggests the two leading positions are not far apart in substance.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the collateral-price mechanism as sufficiently distinct from the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises, and whether citation wording alone can separate them.
Where the credit boundary lies between Kiyotaki-Moore and the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist accelerator, and whether leaving out Gertler and Gilchrist understates the quantitative policy-model lineage.
How much weight indirect empirical identification of the collateral channel should carry against directly tested results such as B005.

For B005, whether Helpman's marginal credit independent of Krugman's 2008 recognition and of his separate B020 entry is large enough, and how far the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum can be handled by wording.
Whether any coherent two-part pairing exists under the three-person cap. I have not found one that does not weaken the clean attribution of B011, so I treat a single part as the working assumption.
My assessments rely on general knowledge and the supplied committee text, and I have not independently verified any source.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for the preferred part. It lists no co-authorship or institutional tie to Kiyotaki, Moore, Gertler, Gilchrist or the credited names in B005. For B012, my alternative, I note that my work with Lindvall and Cermeño on state capacity and railroads is a field adjacency to Persson, Tabellini and Besley and not a personal connection, and that Jan Teorell was formerly at Lund. Fredriksson and Teorell refer to a remark about Persson's past committee role. That remark does not appear in the round-1 files I have, so I cannot assess it. Conflicts are disclosed here and not adjudicated, and I apply common criteria across fields.
